checkpoints.description: [1/2] Reopen a conversation over ACP and let an editor choose its mode. The ACP agent advertises loadSession false and always runs Build, so an editor that restarts loses the conversation it was working in, and a client can never ask for the read-only Plan mode. Pin both behaviours with failing tests first: initialize advertises loadSession, session/load validates cwd and session, replays the stored prose as user/agent message chunks, and continues with a prompt; session/new reports the available modes, session/set_mode switches between Build and Plan, and the next run uses the selected mode.

impact_assessment.why: An editor that restarts cannot reopen the conversation it was in, and ACP advertises that gap as loadSession false, so the only agent surface documented as not supporting resume stays that way.
impact_assessment.benefits: A reopened conversation keeps its history and context, Plan mode becomes reachable from an editor, and the advertised capability matches what the agent implements.
impact_assessment.risks: contract: initialize reports loadSession true and session/new/session/load gain a modes object; dependency: none; concurrency: the sessions map is per process and a load during a running turn keeps the run lease; state: replay reads stored messages without writing any
impact_assessment.mitigation: Test-first on the protocol surface, then the implementation; replay uses the existing listMessages default so tool rows stay hidden; docs and a new ADR record what is now supported and what still is not

Add scripts/ui-clickmap.mjs (npm run ui:clickmap): it drives the running UI through every workspace tab, a new conversation and the terminal drawer, records each testid with the postcondition it verified, lists each visible control it did not drive as a skip with the reason, and exits non-zero when nothing could be driven. Remove the README tree entry for shots/ (a fresh tree has no such directory) and document the new command.

[2/2] Stop two shell-task probes from failing on a loaded host. The ceiling probe waited a fixed 2.5 s for 1 MB of output and the bounded-read probe relied on vitest's 10 s default for a 60,000-line command, so the same code passed on a quiet host and timed out on a busy one (measured: the identical suite took 218 s and 353 s). Poll for the ceiling note itself up to 20 s and give the 60k-line probe its own 60 s bound; no assertion is weakened, and a log that never reaches the ceiling still fails.

impact_assessment.why: The compat gate demanded evidence that did not exist, and two integration probes measured host speed rather than behaviour, so a green run depended on what else the machine was doing.
impact_assessment.benefits: The compat proof is produced by the project itself and names what it really drove, and the shell-task tests assert the same things at any host speed instead of failing under load.
impact_assessment.risks: contract: adds npm script ui:clickmap, leaves compat.json unchanged, no production code touched; dependency: none beyond the existing playwright-core and browser helper; concurrency: the clickmap script starts and stops its own temporary server; state: writes only the git-ignored .aikit/clickmap.log, and the test change only raises its own timeout and polls
impact_assessment.mitigation: The clickmap fails loudly when nothing was driven and its skip lines name why; the ceiling probe still fails when the notice never appears; the whole tree passed 12/12 gates with both changes in place, and the shell-task file was re-run alone after the edit

checkpoints.description: [1/1] Make stopping a run stop its in-flight shell. Analysed projects/harness against atelier: most of the harness's ideas are already here (the r0-r9 ladder including injection refusal, budget death and hallucinated-tool refusal; doom-loop detection; bounded logs; artifact spill; provider failover), but its runner polls the stop switch while a child process runs and kills it, and atelier does not. stopSessionRun aborts the run's AbortController, yet runShell has no signal, so a running bash call (timeoutMs up to 600000) keeps running after the UI says stopped and executeRun stays pending until it exits. Thread the run's signal through executeTool into runShell: on abort kill the process tree, resolve the tool with 'stopped by stop request', and return the run as blocked with reason stopped as soon as the tool result is recorded. Test-first: an aborted run settles in seconds instead of waiting for its 30 s command, and a normal command still completes.

impact_assessment.why: Harness analysis found one capability gap that matters for a local agent: a stop that leaves the command it started running is not a stop, and the run stays pending behind it.
impact_assessment.benefits: Stop means stop for foreground commands too; the run settles in seconds, the process tree is killed, and the transcript records why the call ended.
impact_assessment.risks: contract: executeTool gains an optional signal argument and ToolContext an optional signal field, both backwards compatible; dependency: none; concurrency: an abort listener per shell call, removed when it settles; state: one extra tool.result output line (stopped by stop request)
impact_assessment.mitigation: Test-first at both levels (executeTool with a signal and a real run stopped through stopSessionRun); killing reuses the existing taskkill process-tree helper; a normal command and the existing timeout path are re-run by the full suite

Removing the abort listener again makes both fail by timeout, so the listener is the thing under test. A normal command still runs, and the existing timeout, background-task, streaming and ACP suites pass. 12/12 gates pass (test, lint, typecheck, build, agent-perf, agent-bench, a11y, browser, hygiene, guidelines, secrets, compat). Harness analysis conclusion recorded in ADR-120 and the task plan: the ladder, doom-loop detection, bounded logs, artifact spill and failover were already here; the stop gap was the one behaviour worth porting.

checkpoints.description: [1/1] Stop a run that keeps failing tool calls with different inputs. Fresh harness-vs-atelier pass after the harness reforge: atelier's only loop guard is the doom loop, which fires on an identical call signature (name plus JSON input), so a model that retries with slightly different arguments can burn every step and dollar on calls that all fail (unknown tool, disabled tool, denied approval, a tool exception). Harness stops such a run: its loop counts consecutive failed results and ends the run after two, resetting on any success. Port that guard with a limit of three (atelier's default doomLoopLimit), counting only tool outcomes with ok=false so a failing test command (exit 1, ok=true) never trips it and the fail-fix-test loop still works. Test-first: a run whose model makes three different failing calls ends blocked with a consecutive-failures reason after exactly three tool results, while failures separated by one successful call finish normally.

impact_assessment.why: Fresh harness-vs-atelier pass after the reforge: atelier stops identical repeated calls but not a spiral of different calls that all fail, so a model can burn its whole step and dollar budget on errors.
impact_assessment.benefits: A run that is not converging ends early with a clear reason after three failed calls in a row, and stops costing money; successful calls (including a failing test command, which is a successful tool call) reset the count, so the fail-fix-test loop is untouched.
impact_assessment.risks: contract: one new blocked reason (consecutive tool failures) on the run row and session event; dependency: none; concurrency: the counter is local to the run loop; state: no schema change, no new persistence
impact_assessment.mitigation: Test-first with a fixture provider: three different unknown-tool calls must block after exactly three results, and a failure-success-failure sequence must finish; the constant sits beside the doom-loop check in the same loop; the full suite and gates run after

checkpoints.description: [1/1] Repair the ledger so strict delivery can be proven again. Two bookkeeping defects were blocking `check --strict`: the ACP task's completion had recorded head 5baae1f, which was a later ledger commit, so two consecutive completions shared a head and the check reported "committed nothing" on a task that did commit eeef4df; and the detected-UI-date refresh (71cda6f) had no task owning it, so the completed failure-streak task showed one later non-bookkeeping commit. Set the ACP completion head to the commit it delivered and open this task to own the stamp, with no code changes.

impact_assessment.why: Strict delivery refused a truthful ledger: the ACP completion recorded a later commit as its head, so it looked like a task that committed nothing, and a detection stamp had no owning task so the last completed task looked stale.
impact_assessment.benefits: The ledger records where each task really ended, strict delivery can describe the committed tree again, and nothing in the code or tests changes.
impact_assessment.risks: contract: none, ledger values only; dependency: none; concurrency: the ledger write is atomic and no other writer is active; state: one completion head corrected to the commit the task delivered, plus one task record
impact_assessment.mitigation: The corrected head is the ACP feature commit eeef4df that the task delivered, verified in git; the check that reported the defect is the verifier; the full gate run already passed on this tree
